lead: Move a magnet into a coil and the meter needle jumps; hold the magnet still and the needle falls back to zero. The change in flux, not the flux itself, drives the EMF. Faraday's law states this, and Lenz's law fixes the direction. Inductance turns the idea into a number: flux linkage per ampere. One coil gives self-inductance L; two coils sharing flux give mutual inductance M. This is how transformers, chokes, ignition coils, motor windings and wireless chargers behave, and it is why a winding opposes any sudden change in its current.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.1 for flux, flux density and reluctance, and the phasor picture from Unit 2 for the 90° shift.

sections.h3: Faraday's two laws and Lenz's law

blocks.text: Faraday's first law: an EMF is induced in a coil only while the magnetic flux linked with it is changing. A magnet lying still inside a coil induces nothing. The same magnet pushed in or pulled out induces a pulse, and the faster the push, the bigger the pulse.

blocks.where: e is the induced EMF in volts (V); N is the number of turns of the coil; ΔΦ is the change in flux in webers (Wb); Δt is the time taken in seconds (s).

blocks.text: The product NΦ is called the flux linkage λ, measured in weber-turns. One weber-turn per second is one volt, so the units work out directly. Lenz's law fixes the direction: the induced current sets up its own flux that opposes the change that produced it, which is why the law is written with a minus sign, e = −N·ΔΦ/Δt. Push a north pole towards a coil and the near face turns north and pushes back. Pull it away and the face flips to south and pulls back. Induction always resists.

In a sinusoid this opposition shows up as a 90° shift: the EMF is a cosine while the flux is a sine. Let Φ = Φₘ sin ωt, where Φₘ is the peak flux in webers and ω = 2πf is the angular frequency in rad/s. Then e = −N·Φₘ·ω·cos ωt = N·Φₘ·ω·sin(ωt − 90°). Because of the minus sign, the EMF is a negative cosine, so it lags the flux by 90°. Its magnitude peaks when the flux is zero, and it is zero when the flux is at its peak, because that is the instant the flux stops changing. In a 50 Hz cycle that puts the EMF peaks at 0 ms and 10 ms, and its zeros at 5 ms and 15 ms. See the figure.

blocks.where: L is the self-inductance in henries (H); N is the number of turns; Φ is the flux produced by the coil's own current in webers (Wb); I is that current in amperes (A).

blocks.text: One henry is one weber-turn per ampere, which is the same as one volt-second per ampere. A coil of 1 H develops 1 V across itself when its current changes at 1 A/s.

Chapter 3.1 gives Φ = NI/S, where S is the reluctance of the magnetic path in ampere-turns per weber. Substituting, L = N²/S. More turns help twice, once in the MMF and once in the linking, so L grows as N squared. An iron core raises L because it lowers S.

blocks.where: e is the EMF induced in the coil in volts (V); L is the self-inductance in henries (H); di/dt is the rate of change of the coil's own current in amperes per second (A/s).

blocks.text: The minus sign is Lenz's law again: the coil fights any change in its own current. Rising current gives an EMF opposing the rise; falling current gives an EMF trying to keep it flowing. This is why a motor winding or a transformer primary cannot be switched off instantly — the sudden di/dt makes a large EMF, which arcs across the switch. The energy held is ½Li² joules, and it has to go somewhere.

sections.h3: Mutual inductance M and coupling k

blocks.text: Two coils on one core share flux. When the current in coil 1 changes, part of its flux links coil 2 and induces an EMF there, with no wire between them.

blocks.where: M is the mutual inductance in henries (H); N₂ is the turns of coil 2; Φ₂₁ is the flux from coil 1 that links coil 2 in webers (Wb); I₁ is the current in coil 1 in amperes (A); e₂ is the EMF induced in coil 2 in volts (V); di₁/dt is the rate of change of I₁ in A/s.

blocks.text: Only the part of the flux that actually links both coils counts. The coefficient of coupling k measures that sharing: k = M/√(L₁L₂), with 0 ≤ k ≤ 1. Here k is a pure number, L₁ and L₂ are the self-inductances in henries. k = 1 means all the flux of one coil links the other; k = 0 means none. From this, M can never exceed √(L₁L₂). An iron-core transformer has k close to 1; two small air-cored coils a metre apart have k near 0.

Two coils in series give L = L₁ + L₂ ± 2M, plus when their fluxes aid and minus when they oppose. The dot convention marks this on a diagram: dots go on the two terminals that are the same end, and current entering both dotted ends produces aiding flux. One-line rule — both currents into the dotted ends: use +2M; one into a dot and one out of a dot: use −2M. Only a few syllabi go further into dot-rule algebra; that belongs to a circuits course.

figure.caption: One 50 Hz cycle: the flux peaks at 5 ms and 15 ms. The induced EMF is a negative cosine: its magnitude is largest at 0 ms and 10 ms, when the flux is zero, and it passes through zero exactly when the flux is at its peak. The EMF lags the flux by 90°.

spec.aria: One 50 Hz cycle: the sinusoidal flux peaks at 5 ms and 15 ms. The induced EMF is a negative cosine of the flux, with largest magnitude at 0 ms and 10 ms, when the flux is zero, and zero when the flux peaks; the EMF lags the flux by 90 degrees.

examples.question: (a) A coil of 500 turns has its flux changed uniformly from 2 mWb to 6 mWb in 8 ms. Find the induced EMF. (b) Two coils on one core have L₁ = 0.4 H, L₂ = 0.1 H and k = 0.6. Find M, and the EMF induced in coil 2 when the current in coil 1 rises at 50 A/s.
steps: Convert the units first. Change of flux: ΔΦ = 6 − 2 = 4 mWb = 4 × 10⁻³ Wb. Time: Δt = 8 ms = 8 × 10⁻³ s.
Apply Faraday's second law: e = N·ΔΦ/Δt = 500 × (4 × 10⁻³) ÷ (8 × 10⁻³).
The 10⁻³ factors cancel: 4 ÷ 8 = 0.5, so e = 500 × 0.5 = 250 V.
For M, use the coupling formula: M = k·√(L₁L₂) = 0.6 × √(0.4 × 0.1) = 0.6 × √0.04 = 0.6 × 0.2 = 0.12 H.
The mutual EMF magnitude is e₂ = M·di₁/dt = 0.12 × 50 = 6 V. By Lenz's law it opposes the rise of current in coil 1.
examples.answer: The induced EMF is 250 V; the mutual inductance is M = 0.12 H and the EMF in coil 2 is 6 V.
examples.check:
N = 500
dphi = (6 - 2) * 1e-3
dt = 8e-3
e = N * dphi / dt
print(round(e, 6))
L1 = 0.4
L2 = 0.1
k = 0.6
M = k * (L1 * L2) ** 0.5
print(round(M, 6))
di1_dt = 50
e2 = M * di1_dt
print(round(e2, 6))

traps: Dropping N. Using ΔΦ/Δt alone gives 0.5 V instead of 250 V; the turns multiply the answer.
Unit slip: mWb must become ×10⁻³ Wb and ms must become ×10⁻³ s. Missing one factor puts the answer a thousand times off, and examiners deduct the unit mark too.
'Uniformly' means the answer from ΔΦ/Δt is the average EMF. For a non-uniform change you must use e = −N·dΦ/dt at the instant asked for.
Mixing up M and k. k is a dimensionless number between 0 and 1; M is in henries and can never exceed √(L₁L₂). Also M is the same both ways: M₁₂ = M₂₁.
Writing L = L₁ + L₂ + 2M without looking at the dots. If the two fluxes oppose, the correct total is L₁ + L₂ − 2M, and the sign is the whole point of the question.

quiz.q: State Faraday's two laws of electromagnetic induction.
quiz.a: First law: an EMF is induced in a coil whenever the flux linked with it changes. Second law: e = N·ΔΦ/Δt, with N the turns, ΔΦ in webers and Δt in seconds.
A coil has 1 H of self-inductance when its flux linkage is 1 weber-turn per ampere of its own current; equivalently, when it develops 1 V as its current changes at 1 A/s.

quiz.q: Why does Faraday's law carry a minus sign?
quiz.a: Lenz's law: the induced current produces a flux that opposes the change in flux that caused it. The minus sign records that opposition of direction, not a negative magnitude.

quiz.q: The flux through a coil is at its maximum value. What is the induced EMF at that instant, and why?
quiz.a: Zero. At a peak the flux is momentarily not changing, so dΦ/dt = 0. The EMF is largest at the zero crossings of the flux.

quiz.q: A coil of 200 turns links a flux that changes from 0.5 mWb to 2.5 mWb in 4 ms. Find the average induced EMF.
Two coils have L₁ = 0.8 H, L₂ = 0.2 H and k = 0.5. Find M and the EMF induced in coil 2 when the current in coil 1 falls at 10 A/s.
quiz.a: M = k√(L₁L₂) = 0.5 × √0.16 = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2 H. Then |e₂| = M × di₁/dt = 0.2 × 10 = 2 V, with a direction that opposes the fall in current.

quiz.q: Two identical coils are connected in series, first aiding and then opposing, and the total inductance is measured both times. Explain why the two readings differ by 4M.
quiz.a: Aiding gives L = L₁ + L₂ + 2M and opposing gives L = L₁ + L₂ − 2M. Subtracting, the difference is 4M, so M = (L_aid − L_opp)/4. This is a standard laboratory method for finding M without knowing k.

beyond: Not for the exam. Coupled coils are the working principle of wireless phone chargers and electric-vehicle inductive charging pads, where k is deliberately kept small and a resonant capacitor makes up for the weak coupling. Rogowski coils measure lightning and fault currents through mutual inductance with an air core, so they never saturate. Inside machines, the coupling between phases shapes the torque ripple of a brushless drive. Search 'mutual inductance wireless power transfer' and 'Rogowski coil integrator' to go further.
